title: Bansī Vigyān
subtitle: The Science of the Bānsurī — making, practice and performance
author: Pt. Uma Kant Pathak
copyright: All rights reserved by the author
summary: Pt. Uma Kant Pathak ji of Kanpur is a teacher of Hindustani music theory, and of all Indian instruments, particularly the bānsurī (the Indian bamboo flute): its making, playing and performance. In this book he sets down 30 years of bānsurī practice as Sanskrit ślokas with his Hindi commentary. After a salutation come making (every length and hole as a proportion of the bore), practice (breath, tongue, fingers, alaṅkāras, tānas) and performance (tāla, gat, tihāī, rāga profiles, his interval-number notation).

khandas.title: Invocation and Praise
khandas.summary: Opens with a salutation to the bānsurī that rests on Govinda's lips like a second Rādhā, then praises it: the transverse bānsurī (Kṛṣṇā) is as dear to music lovers as the Gītā, its practice brings the four aims of life, and it is sweet, cheap, light and within everyone's reach.

subsections.title: Invocation
subsections.summary: A single salutation verse to the bānsurī: pressed by Govinda's leaf-like fingers and seated on his lips, hollow like a self free of deceit, it is honoured as a second Rādhā.

subsections.title: In Praise of the Bānsurī
subsections.summary: Four verses in praise of the bānsurī. It stands among instruments as the Gītā among scriptures and the Gaṅgā among rivers; the transverse bānsurī (Kṛṣṇā) is as dear to music lovers as the Gītā; its practice yields the four aims of life; and it is sweet, cheap, light and open to rich and poor alike.

khandas.title: Part One: Making the Bānsurī
khandas.summary: How to make a bānsurī. Pathak ji traces its origin and three kinds, ranks materials (seasoned bamboo best), and gives every length and hole size as a proportion of the bore's inner circumference. He places twelve notes by successive division, then adds a simpler second method, artificial komal notes and a bīn-like buzz.

subsections.title: The Origin of the Bānsurī
subsections.summary: Pathak ji's account of the bānsurī's origin: wind sounding broken bamboo in the forest made the first single-note, 'god-made' bānsurī; forest-dwellers copied it and cut holes; Śrī Kṛṣṇa set seven notes in it, earlier bānsurīs giving three; later a fipple was added, easier to play but, he argues, limiting the tone.

subsections.title: The Kinds of Bānsurī and Suitable Materials
subsections.summary: Names the three kinds of bānsurī (Tripurā, Kṛṣṇā, Jihvāvatī) and ranks materials from iron through copper and silver to wood, with well-seasoned bamboo best. Then the base rule: measure the bore's inner circumference with a paper ring; a tube eight to nine times that is best, and under six times will not make a bānsurī.

subsections.title: Placing the Notes
subsections.summary: Places the twelve notes: the open end and a mark 4/10 down from the mouth-hole sound an octave apart, and each other note goes midway, or at equal divisions, between notes already set. Also: enlarging flat holes, shrinking sharp ones, moving holes for the fingers, hole sizes as fractions of the circumference, tuning by ear.

subsections.title: Other Kinds of Bānsurī
subsections.summary: Weighs the three bānsurīs: the Jihvāvatī is easy but unhygienic, its breath and tone set by the maker; the Kṛṣṇā is hard at first, then best; the Tripurā is easy to make, hard to blow. Then six- to nine-hole bānsurīs, Pathak ji's measurements, lengths by harmonium key, the limits of calculation and the 'bound' Pa.

subsections.title: A Second Method of Making
subsections.summary: A simpler method Pathak ji uses himself: divide the length from the mouth-hole to the low Pa into six equal parts, then split the lowest four sixths into two, three, four and five parts to place twelve notes, komal Dha up to Pa. For tubes seven or eight times the circumference, use sevenths instead.

subsections.title: Artificial Komal Notes
subsections.summary: Pathak ji's fix for komal Re and Dha, which are hard to get by half-lifting a finger: narrow those holes with a plug, such as a rosary bead whose small hole is widened while testing on Bhairav or Toḍī, or with a piece of pipe that turns over the holes or slides inside the tube.

subsections.title: The Sound of the Bīn from the Bānsurī
subsections.summary: How to make the bānsurī buzz like a bīn (the snake-charmer's mahuar): cut a second hole near the mouth-hole and cover it with bhojpatra, the thin white membrane inside fresh bamboo. On a transverse bānsurī the hole can go through the cork, with a second cork as an on-off switch; weather affects the membrane.

khandas.title: Part Two: Practice
khandas.summary: Training the player. Breath, tongue (ṭa–ka) and fingers are drilled separately, then together: blowing, fingering, mūrchanā, and ascent–descent in rhythm. Then alaṅkāras, the eleven elements of tāna, the rules of ālāpa (vādī–saṃvādī, four kinds of pause), and worked elaborations of Yaman, Bhūpālī, Bahār and two Sāraṅgs.

subsections.title: Here Begins the Section on Practice
subsections.summary: Opens the practice section. Sādhanā joins body, mind and breath; the learner keeps a simple, disciplined life and an attitude of faith rather than envy, and trains three things: breath through prāṇāyāma, the tongue through the syllables ṭa and ka, and the fingers through exercise.

subsections.title: Practice of the Breath
subsections.summary: A short note on breath: Pathak ji recommends bhastrikā prāṇāyāma (rapid breathing in and out) on winter mornings, two minutes rising to five, so that the tone gains a steady, regular vibration instead of an uneven flicker.

subsections.title: Practice of the Tongue and of the Fingers
subsections.summary: The core drills: ṭa–ka tonguing and tapping each finger a hundred times; how air vibrates in a bānsurī; three kinds of blowing and ten qualities of a good blow, first practised at a fire; fingering six and nine holes; bānsurī sizes; mūrchanā and ascent–descent in rhythm; then varṇas, sparśa and mīṇḍ.

subsections.title: The Definition of Alaṅkāra
subsections.summary: Defines the alaṅkāra: a pattern of a few notes carried in rhythm through the whole ascent and descent. Its qualities are repetition, reversal, skipping and wandering, fitting a tāla, and following the long and short syllables of words; tables give examples and practice alaṅkāras of four to sixteen beats.

subsections.title: The Elements of Tāna
subsections.summary: Lists the eleven elements of tāna, from skipping and turning back to mixed tempos and repetition, with examples. Then extending a pattern through all notes (tables in Rūpak, Dādrā, Kaharvā, Tīntāl), ālāpa and Sa as its resting point, vādī–saṃvādī, four kinds of pause, and five actions of elaboration.

subsections.title: Some Ālāps in Rāga Yaman
subsections.summary: Three Yaman ālāpas marked with Pathak ji's pause signs. Then svasthāna (a fixed note up to its fourth; four across the registers), the guru as cure for doubt, and the marks for rāga outlines: a circle for vādī, a half-circle for saṃvādī, two halves for vivādī, a bar joining paired notes, a snake for oscillation.

subsections.title: Rāga Bhūpālī and Note Elaboration
subsections.summary: Notation only: the marked ascent and descent of Bhūpālī with four svara-vistāras (note elaborations), then the same for Madhyamādi (Madhumād) Sāraṅg with five, using the pause and vādī–saṃvādī signs just introduced.

subsections.title: Rāga Bahār
subsections.summary: Bahār's ascent and descent with four svara-vistāras, and a note on how Pathak ji's pause signs differ from other books. Śloka 126 then sets the order of work: free ālāpa, ālāpa in rhythm (layālāpa), free tānas, and finally tānas set in tāla, like cotton spun into thread and woven into cloth.

subsections.title: Rāga Vṛndāvanī Sāraṅg, Layālāp and Free Tānas
subsections.summary: The three stages in one rāga, Vṛndāvanī Sāraṅg: four svarālāpas, a layālāpa and free tānas, all in notation. Śloka 127: pauses follow the breath, then a chosen beat, then grow fewer at double or triple speed; tānas fitted to a tāla are bound tānas. A devotional verse closes the practice section.

khandas.title: Part Three: Performance
khandas.summary: Playing rāga within tāla. Pathak ji explains how syllable lengths become beats, defines sam, shows how to compose a gat and build tihāīs of any length, and advises mastering one rāga deeply. Bhūpālī and Khamāj are profiled in tables, and songs are written in his own interval-number notation.

subsections.title: Here Begins the Section on Performance
subsections.summary: Opens the performance section: as metre makes speech pleasing, tāla makes rāga so. Pathak ji contrasts bound and unbound singing, shows how timing changes meaning, matches bānsurī tonguing syllables to sitar and tabla bols, separates gat from song, lists kinds of singing, gives rules for syllable length, and defines sam.

subsections.title: How to Compose a Gat
subsections.summary: How to compose a gat: set the rāga's main note on sam with a pause, move toward the saṃvādī, rest on Sa, fill the remaining beats, and start playing from the phrase leading into sam. Bhūpālī examples in Rūpak and Tīntāl follow, then ornamenting, śruti defined, and the kinds and making of tihāīs.

subsections.title: The Qualities of Tihāīs
subsections.summary: The three uses of a tihāī: it completes a tāla cycle when an improvised passage runs short or long, brings out the note on sam, and creates an exchange with the drummer. A table gives tihāīs from three to sixteen beats in Tīntāl, followed by the arithmetic for a chakkardār tihāī spanning several cycles.

subsections.title: Rāgas Especially Suited to the Bānsurī
subsections.summary: Rāgas that suit the bānsurī: easy, sweet ones (Bhūpālī, Pahāḍī, Durgā, Mālkauns, Yaman) and sweet but hard ones (Pīlū, Bhairavī, Darbārī, Pūriyā); holes meant to be half-opened are best made oval. Śloka 147 advises staying with one rāga for a long time, as one digs in one spot to reach water.

subsections.title: Rāga Bhūpālī: Ascent and Descent
subsections.summary: A profile table for Bhūpālī (Kalyāṇ thāṭ, pentatonic, Ga–Dha as vādī–saṃvādī, first watch of the night, calm and grave) with its ascent, descent and pakaḍ. Śloka 148 sets the working order: split the scale by register into small groups, elaborate, add rhythm, carry it into tālas, then compose a song or gat.

subsections.title: Svara Saṅghāta: Note Combinations
subsections.summary: Mostly tables: four-beat note clusters (svarasaṃghāta) in Bhūpālī, from two and three notes, then grouped by first and last note (Ga to Sa, Pa to Pa, Sāṃ to Ga and others). Words guide the tongue, ṭa falling only on syllables; it ends with practice for a rāga with śuddha Ni up and komal Ni down.

subsections.title: An Introduction to Rāga Khamāj
subsections.summary: A profile table for Khamāj (its own thāṭ, hexatonic up and heptatonic down, Ga–Ni vādī–saṃvādī, playful in mood). Then how learning grows (imitation, the guru's grace, practice, good company), copying songs heard by ear, and the start of Pathak ji's sound-notation: write the syllables by length and dot each rise and fall.

subsections.title: Interval Numbers (Svarāntara Saṅkhyā)
subsections.summary: Pathak ji's interval-number notation: twelve notes have eleven intervals; each number counts from the previous note, upward if written above the syllable, downward if below. Worked songs: 'Om Jai Jagdish Hare', the national anthem (on six holes, 2 is a whole finger, 1 a half hole) and 'Vande Mātaram' in rāga Des.

dedication.text:
To my late, revered father, Śrī Yaduvansh Pathak

who from my childhood awakened in my soul an understanding of Sanskrit and music, and by whose grace I found a place at the feet of eminent gurus: at his ever-remembered feet this small, original booklet is dedicated.

biography.text:
The author: Surmaṇi Pt. Uma Kant Pathak

Born – 11.11.1939
Teaching – music teacher at the IIT Campus School (retired)
★ Bānsurī playing on Ākāśvāṇī (All India Radio), Lucknow, since 1960
★ Author of 'Bansī Vigyān'
★ Inventor of a new nine-hole bānsurī.
★ He set the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā to music.
★ Presented tunes of 326 rāgas, with an introduction to each, on the internet.
★ A fresh outlook on household scientific invention, for example improvements to the hand-pump, the cooler and the telephone.
Honour – 'Surmaṇi' (1978), from the Sur Singār Samiti, Bombay
At present – teacher of vocal music and bānsurī playing at the Lakshmi Devi Lalit Kala Academy
A remarkable wonder – he is able to play the bānsurī for one to one and a half hours sitting in padmāsana (the lotus posture) on flowing water.

(1) I was born in 1939 in the village of Kariyan, Samastipur district, Bihar, the ancient seat of Śrī Udayanācārya ji, in the lap of Śrīmatī Gulab Tara Devi, wife of Pt. Śrī Yaduvansh Pathak, Nyāya-Vyākaraṇācārya and Saṅgīt Ratna. The grounding (saṃskāra) in Sanskrit and music that my father gave me in childhood has remained my wealth. Though I have command of many instruments, the credit for my special love of the bānsurī goes to the mahātmā who, on a pilgrimage to Śrī Jagannāth Purī, suddenly appeared to me as I was going into the temple, gave me a bānsurī and also taught me a beautiful tune. It was as if he had come bearing the blessing of Śrī Jagannāth ji. What followed: wandering about in Kāśī, I found my guru, Śrī Raghunath Prashant, and my sādhanā (practice) went on at his feet for 5 years. In 1978 I also got teaching work at the Śrī Bhatkhande Saṅgīt Mahāvidyālaya. In 1979 the Sur Singār Samiti, Bombay, honoured me with the title of Surmaṇi.

(2) If in this small book some subjects have been left out that inquirers need, or some subjects have come in that, on sound reasoning, deserve to be refuted or thought over, then on whatever subject readers feel any dissatisfaction, they will kindly forgive me and take the trouble to send their views to the author by letter. I shall be grateful to them and shall try to deal with it properly in the second edition.
– Thank you!
Uma Kant Pathak

nivedan.text:
(1) In this age of scientific progress many great minds have spread their rays in different directions, and through this many hardships of human life have been removed. In the world of music too a full store has been built up. Inspired by those great figures, I too, according to my small understanding, am about to offer my work on the bānsurī at the feet of my late, revered father, Pt. Śrī Yaduvansh Pathak, of village and post Kariyan, Samastipur district, Bihar (Bansī Vigyān).

Having received the blessing of my guru, Śrī Raghunath Prashant ji of Vārāṇasī, I have practised the bānsurī for 30 years and made bānsurīs in many different ways. I have had the good fortune of playing the bānsurī from the Lucknow station of Ākāśvāṇī since 1960. Now I am going to write down my experience for the practitioners (sādhakas) to come, so that the bānsurī may advance in the country. What I have understood of the bānsurī scientifically is not enough in itself, so I shall hope that in time to come more light will be shed on this subject.

Mainly three things are considered in the book – (1) making, (2) practice (sādhanā), (3) performance. Besides these there are also some original elements, so that practitioners' practice can be scientific and interesting.

Uma Kant Pathak
